summary: This informational document describes technical mechanisms that regimes use to block or impair Internet traffic. It aims to help designers, implementers, and users understand the properties of protocols that censors exploit. It makes no protocol recommendations and comes from the Privacy Enhancement and Assessment Research Group.

eli5.summary: Some governments try to stop people from reaching parts of the internet. This is a list of the tricks they use, so people who build the internet understand them.

questions: how does deep packet inspection work
subtitle: A technical survey of how regimes block or impair Internet access

tldr.problem: Governments and organizations around the world use various technical mechanisms to block or degrade access to Internet content they deem undesirable.
tldr.mechanism: Censors operate at multiple layers of the network stack and work through three stages: identifying what to censor (prescription), determining which traffic to block (identification), and preventing access (interference). Each stage employs techniques that protocol designers and implementers should understand.
tldr.outcome: Awareness of these mechanisms helps protocol designers build systems more resistant to censorship, while users and circumvention tool developers can understand adversarial capabilities. The RFC makes no policy recommendations, only technical documentation.

today: RFC 9505 is an Informational RFC published in November 2023 as a product of the Privacy Enhancement and Assessment Research Group. It has not been obsoleted and remains the authoritative technical survey of Internet censorship mechanisms. The RFC is referenced by protocol designers considering censorship resistance and by researchers studying censorship systems. Unlike standards that mandate implementation choices, RFC 9505 purely documents existing practices to inform future protocol development.

sections.title: Understanding Internet Censorship
sections.content:
Internet censorship occurs when an entity in a position of power—government, organization, or individual—suppresses communication it considers objectionable or inconvenient. This RFC focuses on technical mechanisms regimes use to block or impair Internet traffic. Unlike RFC 7754, which discusses implications for Internet architecture, this document describes the censorship techniques themselves from a protocol perspective.

Understanding how censors operate helps protocol designers recognize protocol properties that can be exploited for censorship, implementers understand deployment constraints in censorious regimes, and users and tool developers understand adversary capabilities. The RFC represents consensus of the Privacy Enhancement and Assessment Research Group (PEARG) and is purely informational; it makes no policy judgments about which censorship is justified.
sections.eli5: This is a technical guide to how governments block the internet. Knowing how it works helps designers build it better.

sections.title: Three Stages of Censorship
sections.content:
The RFC organizes censorship into three conceptual stages: prescription (determining what types of material to censor), identification (determining which traffic to block), and interference (preventing access). Prescription typically uses blocklists of domains, IP addresses, keywords, or content hashes, or real-time heuristic assessment. Identification happens at multiple network layers—application, transport, and routing—using various packet inspection and metadata analysis techniques. Interference ranges from DNS manipulation to packet dropping to DDoS attacks.

Different censors use different combinations of these stages. A simple censorship regime might maintain a keyword blocklist and block all traffic matching keywords at the application layer. A sophisticated censor like China's Great Firewall performs prescription via multiple channels, identification using deep packet inspection at multiple layers, and interference through packet injection and dropping. Understanding these three stages helps protocol designers recognize which properties of their protocols are vulnerable to censorship at each stage.
sections.eli5: Censors decide what to block (prescription), figure out which traffic is that (identification), and then stop it (interference). Each stage uses different tricks.

sections.title: Identifying Content for Censorship
sections.content:
Censors identify targetted traffic using various network-layer techniques. At the application layer, they inspect unencrypted HTTP headers for domain names and request paths, read TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) fields sent in the clear, and use deep packet inspection (DPI) to search for keywords in encrypted flows by reassembling TCP streams. At the transport layer, they blocklist IP addresses and blocking ports. At the routing layer, they analyze BGP advertisements to misdirect traffic.

The RFC emphasizes that identification techniques exploit protocol properties: HTTP headers and SNI are unencrypted by design to support multi-tenancy. DPI reassembles flows to scan content, requiring significant computational resources but providing powerful identification. DNS queries and responses are typically unencrypted, making DNS a natural identification point. Understanding what protocol properties censors exploit helps designers make informed choices: encrypting SNI makes censorship harder but may push censors to other techniques; using HTTPS/TLS makes application-layer inspection harder but still allows SNI-based blocking.
sections.eli5: Censors look at domain names in unencrypted messages, blocklist IP addresses, or watch the size and timing of encrypted traffic to figure out what you're accessing.

sections.title: Techniques for Blocking Access
sections.content:
Once traffic is identified, censors interfere through various mechanisms. DNS interference redirects domain lookups to wrong IPs or blocks them, affecting all protocols. Packet dropping silently discards traffic matching identified criteria. RST injection forges TCP reset packets to abort connections. Performance degradation (rate limiting) makes connections so slow users abandon them. Network disconnection and BGP hijacking reroute traffic or disconnect regions entirely. Distributed denial of service (DDoS) overwhelms infrastructure. Censors can also take non-technical approaches: manual filtering by human review, pressuring service providers to censor themselves, taking down servers, and domain seizure.

Different interference techniques have different tradeoffs. DNS interference is cheap but easily circumvented with alternative resolvers. IP blocking is crude but requires users to use proxies to circumvent. DPI-based filtering is expensive but powerful. Compelling service providers to censor themselves avoids infrastructure costs and can be very effective, as many services comply with legal orders. The RFC notes that the most effective censorship systems combine technical and non-technical methods: the Great Firewall of China uses DPI-based packet injection, DNS manipulation, and also leverages service provider compliance and self-censorship.
sections.eli5: Censors can make DNS lie, drop your packets, slow your connection down, block whole IP addresses, or pressure websites to censor themselves.

sections.title: Points of Control and Empirical Examples
sections.content:
Censors exploit different points of control in the network: international gateways and Internet Exchange Points (for country-level censorship), ISP networks, institutions, content delivery networks, certificate authorities, service providers, and end-user devices. Each point of control has different capabilities and limitations. Controlling international gateways is very effective for country-level blocking but cannot identify inter-regional traffic. ISPs are frequently exploited through government mandate or coercion. CDNs and certificate authorities are powerful because they are trusted intermediaries that can be forced to issue rogue certificates or revoke legitimate ones.

The RFC provides numerous empirical examples: China's Great Firewall uses DPI to identify and drop traffic, inject RSTs, and poison DNS. Iran throttles HTTPS to encourage HTTP, blocks Tor, and uses SNI-based filtering. Russia blocks ESNI connections entirely. Turkey attempted DNS blocking but users circumvented it with alternative DNS resolvers, forcing ISPs to implement IP blocking. The Kaminsky DNS attack (2008) revealed how lack of port and ID randomization enabled DNS cache poisoning, leading to RFC 5452 requiring DNS ID and port randomization. These examples show that censorship capabilities are real, sophisticated, and evolving as both censors and circumvention tool developers innovate.
sections.eli5: Different countries use different tricks. Some are cheap and easy to bypass. Others are expensive but very hard to get around. Censors keep inventing new tricks as people find workarounds.

sections.title: Implications for Protocol Design and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 9505 is a technical reference, not a policy document, but it has clear implications for protocol designers and implementers. Protocol designers should understand which properties of their protocols can be exploited for censorship and make conscious choices about tradeoffs: encrypting metadata makes censorship harder but may have performance or interoperability costs; always using HTTPS resists application-layer censorship but enables SNI-based filtering. Implementers in censorious jurisdictions may need to support circumvention techniques. Users and civil society organizations can use the RFC to understand the sophistication of censorship systems they face.

RFC 9505 is Informational, published in November 2023, from the Privacy Enhancement and Assessment Research Group. It is not a Standards Track document and makes no protocol recommendations. Instead, it provides a detailed taxonomy and empirical examples to help the Internet community understand censorship as a technical challenge. Future protocol work addressing censorship resistance (like Encrypted Client Hello for TLS) can reference the RFC to justify design choices. The RFC itself points to ongoing work in circumvention and notes that the interaction between censors and tool developers is an active research area.
sections.eli5: This RFC helps protocol designers understand how their design choices make censorship easier or harder. It's a reference, not rules, but it's very useful for making better choices.
